body.text: Trade & investment , explained.
A new international treaty strengthens Australia’s case for domestic reform – but only if major economies sign on too.

Global demand for authentic Indigenous products, art and knowledge has helped position First Nations culture and intellectual property as a growing element of Australia’s international engagement, complementing efforts to strengthen partnerships and expand economic ties across the region . What remains missing is not goodwill towards First Nations cultural assets, but a functioning intellectual property regime .

Internationally, Australia is progressing towards ratification of the World Intellectual Property Organisation’s Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge Treaty . It marks a milestone for Indigenous recognition in global intellectual property law as the first treaty to address the intersection of patents and traditional knowledge while including provisions specific to Indigenous peoples . The treaty is focused on patent disclosure requirements relating to genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge.

But momentum remains slow, with only four countries, Malawi, Uganda, Peru and Albania, having ratified . Without the major manufacturing economies participating in the treaty, there is a risk that Australian ratification concentrates new compliance and disclosure obligations on small and medium-sized enterprises while doing little to constrain those operating outside the treaty.

Domestically, Australia’s cultural policy “ Revive ” has focused on strengthening traditional knowledge protections through new legislation, bolstering the Indigenous Art Code, improving funding arrangements, increasing professional support and development opportunities and progressing work towards dedicated Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property legislation . The reforms respond in part to a 2022 Productivity Commission report , which found two-thirds of “Indigenous-style” souvenirs sold in Australia were inauthentic and recommended stronger protections for Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property .

Yet past attempts at protection and certification schemes have introduced unforeseen burdens and costs on the very organisations they were designed to protect . Fair trade certification , for example, set out to protect producers who had been squeezed out of the value of their own goods . In practice, the burden of proving compliance has fallen on producers themselves, who face intense scrutiny to maintain the scheme’s ethical standards .
What remains missing is not goodwill towards First Nations cultural assets, but a functioning intellectual property regime.

Verifying where a product actually originated , and meeting the technical standards a deal requires, can erode the competitiveness those deals are meant to create, particularly for smaller businesses least able to absorb the paperwork . Recent analysis by Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation similarly notes that restrictive rules of origin can challenge micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises with limited capacity to manage complex compliance requirements.

While the treaty is focused on genetic resources, patent disclosure and associated traditional knowledge, similar questions surrounding attribution, authenticity and benefit-sharing emerge across broader Indigenous cultural and intellectual property debates. Tensions are already visible in Indigenous cultural industries. Authentic Indigenous businesses may bear the costs of maintaining cultural authority, attribution and authenticity while competing against inauthentic Aboriginal-style products manufactured or sold outside of Australia. For example:

The treaty may contain a blind spot, one that could turn a miracle into a mirage . The treaty’s disclosure requirements address longstanding concerns about the use of genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge used in patent applications . But genetic resources and traditional knowledge are progressively being digitised, shared and reused without anyone interacting with the communities from which they originated .

For example, a pharmaceutical company may be required to disclose the origin of a genetic resource or associated traditional knowledge used in research, but once that information is sequenced, digitised and shared as data, questions emerge about how disclosure, attribution and benefit-sharing obligations should continue to apply .

Emerging AI technologies further risk amplifying this dynamic . AI systems can reproduce and commercialise Indigenous cultural expressions without engaging the communities from which they originate, raising questions of attribution, consent and benefit-sharing as cultural value becomes economic value . More recently, Wandjina imagery has again appeared in social media posts identified as AI-generated and not created in Australia , causing considerable distress to the Mowanjum community and underlining the continued challenge of protecting culturally significant material reproduction once it moves beyond traditional custodial control.

The challenge for policymakers is not necessarily the number of rules, but whether they can be enforced consistently and applied broadly enough to avoid creating incentives for free riding. Ratification of the traditional knowledge treaty strengthens the case for Australian domestic policy reforms by linking Australia’s domestic arrangements to emerging international obligations.
But getting major manufacturing economies to participate in the treaty will also be key.
Mathew Kerwin

Mathew Kerwin is a Lowy Institute First Nations Fellow. He is a proud Worimi Nation man of the Forster–Tuncurry region, New South Wales, and a descendant of the great Lester (Charlie) Leon, son of Dr Dale Kerwin.
